title: Managing GlusterFS Without Losing the CLI: Introducing the Eliware Operator Console
summary: A tour of the Eliware GlusterFS operator console for cluster health, volumes, files, permissions, NFS-Ganesha, and audited day-to-day operations.
author: Eliware
content:
# Managing GlusterFS Without Losing the CLI: Introducing the Eliware Operator Console

GlusterFS gives storage operators a powerful command-line interface, but operating a cluster involves more than remembering individual commands. You also need a reliable view of peers, bricks, volumes, mounts, access permissions, audit history, recovery state, and the clients using the storage.

The Eliware GlusterFS Operator Console is a web-based control surface for those everyday tasks. It is designed to make the cluster easier to see and safer to operate without pretending that a graphical interface can replace storage knowledge.

The console does not hide the GlusterFS model. It puts that model in one place:

- peers are still peers;
- bricks remain node-local storage paths;
- volumes retain their GlusterFS identities;
- replica and failure behavior still require testing; and
- destructive operations remain administrative actions.

## What the console is for

The console is intended for operators managing a small GlusterFS cluster alongside applications or platform infrastructure. It provides a central dashboard for the status and operations that otherwise require a mixture of CLI commands, filesystem checks, service inspection, and application-specific procedures.

From the dashboard, an authenticated operator can inspect:

- cluster and peer health;
- console-node reachability;
- volume state and brick status;
- NFS-Ganesha state and exports when enabled;
- recent GlusterFS log lines;
- basic Prometheus-compatible metrics;
- snapshots, quotas, options, profiles, and heal information;
- mounted volume contents; and
- the audit history of administrative activity.

The goal is not to create a second storage abstraction that operators must learn. The goal is to make the existing storage state visible enough that an operator can make a better decision before running a command.

## A central view of a distributed cluster

A three-node GlusterFS cluster has state distributed across the nodes. A single browser request should not require an operator to guess which node currently has the useful answer.

The console can discover configured Gluster peers and aggregate their status into a central view. Console-node identity is stable, so supervisor actions can be directed to the intended node even when the dashboard itself is reached through a shared route.

That distinction matters during maintenance. If a node is intentionally restarting, the rest of the status view should remain useful. If a service exits unexpectedly, the console reports the degraded condition and the supervisor can apply its configured recovery behavior.

This is operational visibility, not magic failover. The underlying GlusterFS peers, bricks, volumes, network paths, and Kubernetes scheduling decisions still determine what the cluster can do.

## Volumes without asking ordinary operators for brick paths

Creating a GlusterFS volume traditionally requires careful knowledge of the brick set and server-side paths. That is appropriate for cluster administrators, but it is also an easy place for a routine application request to become a storage-layout mistake.

The Eliware console takes a narrower approach for normal volume creation:

1. An operator supplies a display name.
2. The console uses the configured Gluster peers.
3. It derives one brick path per peer below the configured node-local brick root.
4. It creates a replica-3 application volume.
5. It records ownership and operational metadata separately from the GlusterFS internal name.

The display name is metadata. It can be changed without renaming the underlying GlusterFS volume. That makes an application-facing name safe to correct later without creating a storage migration event.

The protected internal `gluster` volume is kept separate. It stores shared console state and is never treated as an ordinary application volume. A media, backup, or repository workload gets its own application volume rather than sharing the control-plane data volume.

This separation is one of the most important design rules in the project:

> Shared control-plane state and application data should have different operational boundaries.

## File operations with a volume boundary

The console includes a file explorer for mounted GlusterFS volumes. It supports browsing, details and icon views, uploads, downloads, folder creation, copy and move operations, and bounded text-file editing.

The explorer does not read brick directories directly. It works through mounted volumes, which preserves GlusterFS coordination and keeps server-side brick layout out of the normal user experience.

File operations are deliberately bounded:

- uploads are streamed through the HTTP/filesystem path;
- upload size is limited by configuration;
- text editing has a smaller explicit size limit;
- paths are normalized;
- symlinks are rejected; and
- administrative file operations are audited.

These limits are not intended to turn a browser into a general-purpose bulk-transfer system. They make the explorer useful for operational tasks while keeping large transfers on an appropriate filesystem or data pipeline.

## Access control that follows the volume

A storage dashboard should not assume that every authenticated user should see every volume. The console supports a root administrator and scoped users with volume-specific permissions.

A scoped user may receive permissions such as:

- read;
- write;
- settings; or
- delete.

A user can also have permission to create volumes without automatically receiving access to every existing volume. Volume ownership and explicit grants determine the scope of routine application access. The protected shared-state volume remains restricted from scoped users.

This is intentionally different from putting a password prompt in front of a fully open administrative API. Authentication, authorization, network policy, and trusted routing all matter. The administrative API should remain behind internal routing and should not be exposed publicly.

Set unauthenticated mode only for a deliberately trusted local compatibility test. It should not be the default for a deployed operator console.

## Dangerous actions stay visible

Storage interfaces become dangerous when they make destructive operations look like ordinary form submissions. The console keeps high-risk operations explicit:

- deleting a volume removes its underlying GlusterFS volume and data;
- removing or replacing a brick changes the storage topology;
- restoring shared state replaces selected persisted files;
- changing volume options can affect existing workloads; and
- supervisor controls can stop a GlusterFS service on a selected node.

The protected shared `gluster` volume cannot be deleted through the ordinary volume lifecycle. Delete permissions are scoped and authenticated. Operational actions are recorded in the audit log.

The interface does not eliminate the need for confirmation, backups, maintenance windows, or change review. It makes the consequences easier to see before an operator proceeds.

## Readiness is different from liveness

The console exposes separate health concepts because a process being alive is not the same as storage being ready.

- `/healthz` answers whether the process is alive.
- `/readyz` answers whether the required storage and cluster conditions are available.
- `/api/status` provides a more detailed operator view.

Readiness can require a live GlusterFS daemon, connected peers, a started volume, online bricks, and an available shared-state mount when shared state is required. A healthy Node.js process should not announce storage readiness when the volume it depends on is unavailable.

This distinction is especially useful in Kubernetes. A liveness probe should not restart a process merely because a dependency is temporarily degraded. A readiness probe should prevent traffic from being sent to a console that cannot safely serve its required state.

## NFS-Ganesha is optional

The console can report NFS-Ganesha state and manage configured exports when the deployment includes a validated Ganesha and Gluster FSAL layer. NFS is not automatically enabled just because GlusterFS packages are installed.

Native GlusterFS clients and NFS clients are different access paths. The native client uses GlusterFS discovery and direct brick connections. NFS clients connect to Ganesha, which translates requests through the configured FSAL. Each path needs its own network, authentication, performance, and failure testing.

The local Compose topology leaves NFS disabled by default. That keeps the base storage test focused and avoids implying that an optional protocol layer is present when it has not been deliberately configured.

## What the console does not promise

The console is not:

- a replacement for GlusterFS documentation;
- a backup system;
- a database administration console;
- a public-facing storage API;
- a way to safely edit brick contents directly; or
- proof that a volume is suitable for every workload.

The shared `gluster` volume is intentionally low-throughput control-plane storage. It is not a recommendation to place SQLite or another database on GlusterFS without workload-specific testing. Application data belongs in separate volumes with their own capacity, performance, access, and backup decisions.

## Built around the native storage model

The best management layer is one that helps operators understand what is happening underneath. The Eliware console therefore keeps the important boundaries visible:

```text
Authenticated operator
          │
          ▼
  Eliware operator console
          │
   ┌──────┼────────┐
   ▼      ▼        ▼
 peers  volumes  files
   │      │        │
   └──────┴────────┘
          ▼
      GlusterFS
          ▼
 node-local bricks
```

The dashboard gives operators a coherent place to inspect and request changes. GlusterFS remains responsible for the distributed filesystem. The node-local filesystems remain responsible for storing bricks. Kubernetes remains responsible for scheduling and persistent-volume placement.

Those boundaries are a feature. They make it possible to reason about failures instead of hiding every layer behind a single “storage healthy” label.

## Try it carefully

The project is experimental and its deployment artifacts remain environment-specific. If you want to evaluate the console, start with the local three-node Compose topology and a temporary bootstrap password. Use disposable data, keep the administrative route trusted, and run the authenticated lifecycle checks before considering a deployment.

Begin with the [EL10 installation and first-volume guide](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/), then use the official [GlusterFS architecture documentation](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Quick-Start-Guide/Architecture/) to understand the storage model behind the dashboard.

The purpose of the console is simple: make GlusterFS easier to see, easier to operate deliberately, and harder to misunderstand.
